title: Pauline Hanson clarifies One Nation migration policy after MP's mix-up
text:
By NICHOLAS COMINO, POLITICAL REPORTER, AUSTRALIA

Published:  16:18 AEST, 27 August 2026   |  Updated:  08:18 AEST, 30 August 2026

60

View  comments

Pauline Hanson has clarified One Nation's migration policy after one of her MPs publicly contradicted the party's position.

On Sunday, One Nation MP David Farley suggested the party's stance was 'similar' to Labor's migration settings.

But on Thursday, Hanson insisted the party's proposed cap of 130,000 applies only to permanent migrants who could ultimately become Australian citizens, not temporary visa holders.

'Those people we're going to give permanent residency and who can move on to citizenship, that's at 130,000,' she said while speaking in Dubbo alongside Nationals Leader Matt Canavan at the Daily Telegraph's Bush Summit.

She stressed temporary visa holders would not be included in the figure, including workers under the Pacific Australia Labour Mobility (PALM) scheme.

'On top of that, you can have your PALM workers and other visa holders in the country,' Hanson said.

Hanson accused Labor of letting temporary migration reach unsustainable levels, arguing that population growth was straining housing and infrastructure.

'We've got three million visa holders in Australia. We're full,' she said.

Pauline Hanson clashed with Matt Canavan over migration policy at the Bush Summit in Dubbo

Pauline Hanson said One Nation's policy is a cap of 130,000 permanent migrants per year

'The foreign students, the graduates, postgraduates and all their families they bring in, that needs to be cut back.'

Asked whether Farley had been wrong in his comments, Hanson said he had mixed up permanent migration with temporary visas.

'David Farley got confused about the visa holders,' she said.

'As I've always said, PALM workers are visa holders who can come into the country. They're usually provided accommodation by the farms that employ them.'

Hanson criticised Australia's international education sector, saying universities had become too dependent on foreign students.

Turning to the Coalition's view, Canavan declined to nominate a specific migration target but reiterated that migration should remain below the number of homes being built.

'We've said net overseas migration should be below the number of homes we build and well below for at least the next few years, given the massive surge we've seen under this government,' Canavan said.

'There is no doubt migration numbers have to come down.'

David Farley (pictured) caused confusion over One Nation's migration plan on Sunday

Canavan said One Nation's difficulties during the week showed the dangers of setting a migration number too early.

'I think what we've seen over the past week is that it's a little bit of a folly to set such a number now because One Nation have been very confused about it themselves,' he said.

Canavan added that the Coalition would release a detailed migration policy before the next election after considering factors like housing supply, economic conditions and the federal budget.

'We'll have that number before the next election. We'll make sure all of our policies are properly costed, detailed and fully explained,' he said.

The Nationals Leader also linked migration policy to Australia's economic outlook, warning that debt had become a major concern.

'We (have) over $1trillion in debt. This is now a huge issue for our country,' he said.

Outside the summit, Hanson broadened her attack on the Albanese government, accusing Prime Minister Anthony Albanese of failing to understand regional concerns about renewable energy projects.

'The Prime Minister says he gets it. He hasn't got it,' Hanson said.

She claimed Labor's energy policies had made life harder for farmers, manufacturers and small businesses, and reiterated her support for nuclear power.

'You can't go with this intermittent power from renewables, which is only going to increase your electricity prices over the years,' she said.

Hanson said rising energy costs were hurting households and businesses, while again criticising Climate Change and Energy Minister Chris Bowen.
